sentence: A common sleep problem in which a person regularly has trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or both.
note: NHS: regularly having trouble sleeping; MedlinePlus: hard to fall asleep, stay asleep, or both (summary blended pages).

sentence: Insomnia means regularly having trouble sleeping.
MedlinePlus describes it as a common sleep disorder that can make it hard to fall asleep, hard to stay asleep, or both.
It can last for a short time or continue for months or years.
Daytime tiredness, irritability and poor concentration are among its effects.
Stress, anxiety and depression are the most common causes, according to the NHS.
Changing sleep habits often helps, and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the recommended first treatment when it persists.
note: NHS: changing habits can often help; CBT-I first-line (NHS/StatPearls/NICE scope); blended.

MedlinePlus says good sleep habits often help relieve short-term insomnia.
The NHS suggests going to bed and getting up at similar times each day, and cutting back on caffeine, alcohol and nicotine before bed.
A GP appointment is the usual route if insomnia continues despite changes to sleep habits.
note: NHS: if changing habits does not help, speak to a GP.

sentence: If sleep problems come with thoughts of harming oneself, call 999 or go to A&E if in immediate danger.
note: NHS: call 999 or go to A&E if seriously harmed or about to harm oneself.

sentence: For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, use NHS 111 online or call 111 and choose the mental health option.
Samaritans are free to call on 116 123 at any time of day or night.
Insomnia means having trouble sleeping on a regular basis.
MedlinePlus describes it as a common sleep disorder that makes it hard to fall asleep, hard to stay asleep, or both.
Insomnia can last for a short time, or continue for months or years.
Clinical guidance often separates short-term insomnia, lasting less than three months, from long-term or chronic insomnia, which lasts longer.
note: NICE HealthTech guidance and scope documents.

sentence: Changing sleep habits can often help, and the NHS suggests speaking to a GP if this does not help or if someone thinks they may have insomnia.
Most healthy adults need around seven to nine hours of sleep a night, according to the NHS, although the exact amount differs from person to person.
note: NHS Every Mind Matters sleep problems page.

sentence: NHS guidance for GPs describes insomnia as trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early that affects day-to-day life.
note: BOB ICB guidance (clinic text: impact on day-to-day life).

sentence: Signs of insomnia listed by the NHS include finding it hard to go to sleep, waking several times during the night and lying awake at night.
Other signs are waking up early and being unable to go back to sleep, and still feeling tired after waking up.
During the day, people may feel tired and irritable or find it hard to concentrate.
MedlinePlus says insomnia can cause daytime sleepiness and a lack of energy.
The MedlinePlus encyclopedia adds that it can leave people tired and unfocused, so everyday activities become harder, and that it can raise the risk of car accidents.
A review of chronic insomnia reports links with a higher risk of high blood pressure, depression and anxiety.
note: StatPearls: increased risk of hypertension, depression, anxiety, absenteeism.

sentence: The NHS says the most common causes of insomnia are stress, anxiety and depression.
Other triggers include noise, a room that is too hot or too cold, an uncomfortable bed, and alcohol, caffeine or nicotine.
Jet lag and shift work can also disturb sleep.
Some medical conditions can bring on insomnia, including restless legs syndrome, an overactive thyroid and the menopause.
Mental health conditions, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and some medicines are also listed.
Local NHS guidance for GPs adds that other causes to look for include obstructive sleep apnoea, body-clock disorders and side effects of medicines.
MedlinePlus lists having a lot of stress, a lower income and travelling long distances across time zones as risk factors.
A GP will try to establish the cause of the sleep problem so that treatment can be matched to it.
Clinicians may check for depression, anxiety and other conditions that can affect sleep.
Sleep diaries and questionnaires such as the Insomnia Severity Index may be used.
Guidance describes a sleep diary kept for a week or two as a way of recording total sleep time, time awake after falling asleep and patterns that suggest a body-clock problem.
note: Scope text: sleep diary 7 to 14 days to determine total sleep time, wakefulness after sleep onset, circadian disturbances.

sentence: A diary can also serve as a baseline for judging whether treatment is helping.
One regional guideline says chronic insomnia is managed in primary care before referral to specialists is considered.
note: South Yorkshire/BOB guidelines; summary did not say which.

sentence: Some NHS trusts also run specialist insomnia clinics.
note: Page titles of UCLH and Royal Surrey insomnia clinics.

sentence: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBT-I, is the recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia.
note: NHS, StatPearls and NICE scope; blended.

sentence: The NHS says it can be given face to face by a therapist or through an online self-help programme.
NICE has published guidance on the digital programme Sleepio, which is used to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms.
note: Title of NICE HealthTech guidance HTG624.

sentence: Free NHS CBT-I may not be available in all areas, so the NHS suggests asking a GP.
Good sleep habits often help relieve short-term insomnia, according to MedlinePlus.
Doctors now rarely prescribe sleeping pills for insomnia, because they can have serious side effects and people can become dependent on them.
When they are used, it is usually for a few days or weeks at most, and only if insomnia is severe or other treatments have not worked.
MedlinePlus says most of these medicines can become habit-forming and work less well over time.
The NHLBI says research has not proven melatonin to be an effective treatment for insomnia.
The NHS suggests going to bed and getting up at similar times each day, because this helps the body know when it is time to sleep.
It also suggests avoiding screens for about an hour before bed and cutting back on caffeine, alcohol and nicotine in the hours before sleep.
note: NHS Every Mind Matters; summary blended.

sentence: If someone is still awake after about 20 minutes, the NHS suggests getting up, sitting somewhere comfortable and going back to bed when sleepy.
Writing a to-do list before bed can help when worries about the next day keep someone awake.
One review says the harmful effects of insomnia are largely preventable with appropriate treatment.
Pharmacists can advise on over-the-counter products, although one local NHS guide says these cannot cure insomnia and should not be used for long.
note: Local NHS guide via summary; not from the national page.

sentence: Insomnia that does not improve after changes to sleep habits is a reason to speak to a GP, according to the NHS.
The GP will try to identify the cause, and can explain whether free NHS CBT-I is offered locally.
note: NHS: GP first port of call; free NHS CBT-I may not be available in all areas.
